before.content_html:
Chapter 1: Story of the Door

The novella opens with Mr Utterson and his cousin Richard Enfield on their regular Sunday walk. They pass a mysterious, neglected door in an otherwise respectable street. Enfield tells Utterson a disturbing story: he once saw a small, ugly man trample over a young girl in the street “like some damned Juggernaut.”

The man was Mr Hyde. When confronted, Hyde showed no remorse but agreed to pay compensation. He disappeared through the mysterious door and returned with a cheque signed by Dr Jekyll. Enfield and Utterson agree never to speak of the matter again — a very Victorian response, prioritising discretion over truth.

Key Fact

The trampling of the girl is the reader’s first encounter with Hyde’s violence. Stevenson deliberately makes the victim a child to emphasise Hyde’s complete lack of moral boundaries.

Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

Utterson goes home and reads Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde in the event of Jekyll’s death or “disappearance.” The word “disappearance” troubles Utterson deeply. He visits Dr Lanyon, an old friend of Jekyll’s, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.”

Utterson begins to stake out the mysterious door. When he finally meets Hyde, he is struck by an overwhelming sense of repulsion. He describes Hyde as giving “an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” This is crucial — Hyde’s evil is felt rather than seen.

Throughout the novella, characters struggle to describe what is wrong with Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” Stevenson deliberately makes Hyde’s appearance vague and unsettling. This mirrors the Victorian difficulty in confronting evil directly — they can sense it but cannot name it.

Chapter 3: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

Utterson visits Jekyll at one of his dinner parties. Jekyll is charming, sociable and entirely at ease — the complete opposite of Hyde. When Utterson raises concerns about the will, Jekyll becomes evasive and asks Utterson to drop the subject. He insists: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.”

This chapter establishes the contrast between Jekyll and Hyde. Jekyll is warm, generous and respected; Hyde is cold, violent and repulsive. Yet Jekyll is clearly hiding something — his discomfort when Utterson mentions Hyde reveals the anxiety beneath his polished surface.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s claim that he “can be rid of Mr Hyde” at any time proves tragically wrong. This is an example of dramatic irony — the reader later discovers that Jekyll loses control of the transformations entirely.

Stevenson uses Utterson as the main narrative perspective for most of the novella. As a lawyer, Utterson is rational, restrained and trustworthy — making him a reliable guide for the reader. But his rationality also limits what we can know. He cannot understand Jekyll’s experiment because it is beyond rational explanation. The restricted perspective builds suspense and mirrors Victorian society’s refusal to look too closely at uncomfortable truths.

Stevenson’s Methods in Chapters 1–3

These opening chapters establish several key techniques that Stevenson uses throughout the novella:

Mystery and withholding: Stevenson reveals information slowly. The reader, like Utterson, must piece together clues. The connection between Jekyll and Hyde is not explained until the final two chapters.

Setting as symbolism: The mysterious door — blistered, neglected, with “neither bell nor knocker” — represents the hidden side of Jekyll’s life. It is the back entrance to his laboratory, a passage between his respectable home and his secret world.

Fog and darkness: London is repeatedly described in terms of fog, shadows and gaslight. The fog symbolises the obscured truth and moral confusion at the heart of the story.

before.content_html:
Mr Gabriel John Utterson

Utterson is the novella’s main focaliser for Chapters 1–8. He is a lawyer: rational, loyal and deeply private. Stevenson introduces him as a man of “rugged countenance” who is “lean, long, dusty, dreary” but somehow still “lovable.”

Utterson embodies Victorian respectability. He suppresses his own desires — he enjoys the theatre but has not been to one in twenty years. He drinks gin to “mortify a taste for vintages” (punishing himself for enjoying good wine). He tolerates the failings of others without judging them, preferring to maintain social harmony.

Key Fact

Utterson is a mirror of Jekyll — both repress their desires, but Utterson does so without catastrophic consequences. He represents what Jekyll could have been if he had accepted his limitations rather than trying to transcend them.

Utterson functions as a detective figure. He stakes out Hyde, examines the will, questions Lanyon and eventually breaks down Jekyll’s door. But his Victorian propriety limits his effectiveness — he refuses to open Lanyon’s sealed letter, avoids prying into Jekyll’s private life, and consistently chooses discretion over truth.

This makes Utterson both sympathetic and frustrating. The reader can see clues that Utterson misses or deliberately ignores. Stevenson uses this gap between what the reader suspects and what Utterson knows to build dramatic irony.

Dr Hastie Lanyon

Lanyon is an old friend of Jekyll’s and a fellow doctor. He is described as “hearty, healthy, dapper” and full of confidence. He represents orthodox science — rational, empirical and cautious.

Lanyon dismisses Jekyll’s experiments as “unscientific balderdash.” This disagreement ended their friendship years before the novella begins. When Lanyon finally witnesses Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll, the shock destroys him — he dies within weeks.

Key Fact

Lanyon’s death shows the danger of confronting truths that a person is not prepared for. His rational worldview cannot accommodate what he has seen. Stevenson suggests that some knowledge is too terrible for the human mind to bear — a classic Gothic theme.

Lanyon represents the Victorian scientific establishment — cautious, evidence-based and respectable. Jekyll represents the maverick scientist who pushes beyond accepted boundaries. Their disagreement mirrors real Victorian debates about the limits of science, particularly after Darwin’s theory of evolution challenged religious certainties.

Stevenson does not clearly side with either. Lanyon’s caution is admirable but ultimately leads to ignorance. Jekyll’s ambition is intellectually bold but morally reckless. Both approaches fail.

Richard Enfield

Enfield is Utterson’s cousin and walking companion. He is described as a “well-known man about town” — sociable, worldly and less restrained than Utterson. It is Enfield who tells the story of Hyde trampling the girl in Chapter 1, setting the plot in motion.

Despite being more open than Utterson, Enfield shares the same commitment to discretion. After telling the trampling story, he immediately suggests: “let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.” This instinct to suppress uncomfortable knowledge is central to the novella’s critique of Victorian society.

Poole (Jekyll’s butler) represents the servant class. His loyalty to Jekyll drives the climactic break-in scene. His willingness to act when his master is in danger contrasts with Utterson’s cautious hesitation.

Mr Guest (Utterson’s clerk) notices the matching handwriting. His observational skill as a professional handwriting analyst advances the plot where Utterson’s propriety would not.

The maid who witnesses the Carew murder is one of very few female characters. Her emotional, swooning response contrasts with the male characters’ restraint, reflecting Victorian gender expectations.

before.content_html:
Language: Key Techniques

Stevenson’s language is precise and purposeful. Every word choice contributes to the novella’s atmosphere of mystery, horror and moral unease.

Hyde is consistently described using animalistic imagery. He moves with “ape-like fury,” is called “troglodytic” (cave-dwelling), and shrinks back “with a hissing intake of the breath.” This language links Hyde to degeneration theory — the Victorian fear that humans could reverse-evolve into primitive creatures. By making Hyde animal-like, Stevenson suggests that evil is not a moral failing but a biological reality lurking inside everyone.

Characters repeatedly struggle to describe Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” This technique of describing something by saying it cannot be described is called apophasis. It makes Hyde more terrifying because the reader must imagine the horror for themselves.

This linguistic vagueness also reflects Victorian society’s inability to confront evil directly. The characters can sense that Hyde is wrong, but their respectable vocabulary has no words for what they are feeling.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses pathetic fallacy extensively. London’s fog, darkness and gaslight mirror the moral confusion and hidden evil at the heart of the story. The city itself becomes a character — concealing, distorting and threatening.

Structure: Three Narratives

The novella’s structure is one of its most distinctive features. It uses three different structural layers:

Chapters 1–8: Third-person narrative focused on Utterson. The reader shares his limited perspective, piecing together clues alongside him.

Chapter 9: Lanyon’s first-person letter. A shift to direct testimony from someone who witnessed the transformation.

Chapter 10: Jekyll’s first-person “full statement.” The final revelation, told by the man at the centre of the mystery.

Each narrative layer reveals more of the truth. Utterson sees the outside; Lanyon witnesses the transformation; Jekyll explains everything. This structure mirrors the peeling away of a disguise — the deeper we go, the closer we get to the horrifying reality beneath the respectable surface.

The use of epistolary elements (letters and written statements) is also significant. The truth can only be told in writing, after death. In Victorian society, some truths were literally unspeakable — they could only be committed to paper and sealed away.

Key Fact

The novella ends with Jekyll’s statement, not with Utterson’s reaction. The reader never learns what happens after Jekyll’s death. This open ending forces the reader to draw their own conclusions about the meaning of the story.

Narrative Perspective and Reliability

Stevenson carefully controls what the reader knows and when. Utterson is a reliable narrator in the sense that he reports honestly what he sees. But his perspective is limited — he cannot understand what is happening because it is beyond rational explanation.

Jekyll, by contrast, is an unreliable narrator. Even in his “full statement,” he distances himself from Hyde (“He, I say — I cannot say I”) and minimises his own responsibility. The reader must decide how much to trust Jekyll’s version of events.

Stevenson draws on several Gothic conventions:

The doppelgänger — Hyde is Jekyll’s dark double, a common Gothic motif representing the hidden self.

The mad scientist — Jekyll, like Frankenstein, conducts an experiment that creates a monster beyond his control.

The discovered manuscript — The truth is revealed through found documents (Lanyon’s letter, Jekyll’s statement), a technique used by Gothic writers to create a sense of authenticity.

Atmosphere of dread — Fog, darkness, locked doors and screaming winds create a persistent sense of menace.

glossary_terms.definition: Language that compares a person or thing to an animal, suggesting primitive or uncivilised qualities.
Describing something as indescribable or beyond words, often to heighten its impact on the reader.
The way a text is organised, including its sequence of events, shifts in perspective and use of time.
A narrative told through documents such as letters, diaries or reports rather than a single continuous narration.
A narrator whose account the reader can trust because they have no reason to lie or distort.
A narrator whose account may be biased, incomplete or deliberately misleading.
Established patterns or features that are typical of a particular literary genre.
